title: De-coherent parallel laser processing of ultradense nanopores for high-density, large-area 3D optical phase encoding

paper_content.abstract: Single-beam femtosecond laser pulse scan can surpass the diffraction limit of conventional focusing systems, enabling deep sub-wavelength single-spot modifications via nonlinear absorption at the focus. However, extending this capability to multi-beam parallel processing has been fundamentally limited by the diffraction limit (~λ/2). Herein, we experimentally and theoretically clarify that this limitation stems from spatial coherence and temporal sequence interference, inducing laser-matter interaction crosstalk, non-uniform modifications, and sparse duty-cycle structures. To address this, we propose a de-coherent parallel direct laser writing (Dc-PDLW) strategy, utilizing a patterned single pulse together with a de-coherent holographic algorithm (SSP-BM) to ensure multi-foci polarization orthogonality and eliminate spatial coherence. This method achieves single-shot fabrication of ultra-dense nanopore arrays, with 300 nm (~λ/4) resolution in crystals. We further demonstrate centimeter-scale 3D Pancharatnam–Berry phase plates and voluminous cipher sequences, realizing high-density 3D phase and polarization coding.
paper_content.introduction:
In the field of nanophotonics, the duty cycle emerges as a pivotal metric for quantifying the percentage of the active part in a periodic system. The engineering of duty-cycle in nanostructured elements at the sub-wavelength scale has been demonstrated to enhance the precision of spatial optical phase encoding and structural unit density, thereby enabling unparalleled control of electromagnetic fields1–3. This, in turn, facilitates the integration of high-resolution wavefront shaping4–6, efficient optical phased arrays7, dynamic holographic reconstruction8–10, and multifunctional optical elements11–13. The combination of high-duty-cycle architectures with femtosecond laser direct writing (FLDW) technology demonstrates unique fabrication advantages, including the absence of a mask and the ultra-short pulse characteristics14, which enable non-thermal fusible spatial optical phase encoding with true 3D nanoscale precision in transparent media15–18. This development paves the way for breakthroughs in technologies, such as meta-surface fabrication, LIDAR manufacturing, computational holography, integrated photonic circuits, and optical information encryption, among others.

In the pursuit of efficient spatial optical phase encoding, single-beam processing with femtosecond lasers has been demonstrated to yield sub-wavelength single-spot sizes that overcome the diffraction limit thanks to nonlinear absorption effects19–21. However, in conventional serial laser processing15,22, the structure spacing in unit-by-unit fabrication modes is constrained by light-field redistribution effects arising from spatial coherence. This constraint impedes the fabrication of high-duty-cycle architectures23,24. In consideration of the aforementioned point, the parallel processing using multifocal beams is proposed as a strategy of bypassing the light-field redistribution effects caused by the seed structure to eliminate the spatial coherence. The multi-beam parallel processing can be achieved through various beam-splitting and wavefront-shaping techniques, such as the diffractive optical elements25, the micro-lens arrays26,27, and computational holography based on the Weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS/GSW) iterative algorithm28, and the non-iterative optimal rotation angle algorithm29, the superimposed phase design14. Among these methods, the WGS/GSW iterative algorithm has great flexibility and the best parallel beam uniformity, making it a widely-used method for generating complex multi-beam patterns. However, it is important to note that GSW algorithms do not uniquely determine the phase during the iteration process, which can lead to wavefront disorder that may degrade processing performance30–34, especially under high numerical aperture (NA) focusing conditions. In particular, in the context of this study, where adjacent focal spots are brought into close proximity and their optical fields begin to overlap, this wavefront disorder can induce complex spatial coherence effects, making it difficult to surpass the coherent diffraction limit that constrains the minimum achievable spacing between adjacent spots (≈1.47λ/NA)35. Furthermore, by controlling the polarization orthogonality between adjacent beams, the spatial coherence effects of the optical fields can be effectively eliminated, thereby reducing the minimum achievable spacing between adjacent focal spots by half (≈0.73λ/NA)36, approaching the coherent diffraction limit. However, in multi-focus parallel femtosecond laser processing, the spacing between adjacent focal spots has consistently been constrained by the coherent diffraction limit. In contrast, single-foci parallel femtosecond laser processing, which enables the fabrication of nanostructures with sub-100-nanometer features37–42.

Here, we propose a de-coherent parallel direct laser writing (Dc-PDLW) strategy, leveraging a patterned single pulse and a de-coherent holographic algorithm that combines a stripe segmentation phase hologram with a binary mask (SSP-BM) to eliminate the interaction crosstalk generated by spatial coherence and temporal sequence interference effects, which allows for the machining of large-scale 3D free-designed optical phase encoding in hard and brittle materials. A schematic diagram of multi-foci phase hologram generation and polarization orthogonality is shown in Fig. 1a. The non-iterative strip segmentation phase hologram circumvents the uneven intensity distribution problem under tight focusing, while the binary mask eliminates coherence between adjacent focal spots, together enabling single-shot fabrication of ultra-dense nanopore arrays. A comparison of the minimum dual-pore spacing achieved by different algorithms is presented in Fig. 1b. With the SSP-BM algorithm, we achieve machining of nanostructures at high-duty-cycle, as well as dense linear array structures. Subsequently, it is demonstrated that the strength of the birefringence effect increases as the dual-pore spacing decreases, which also signifies that there is an augmentation in the capabilities of optical phase encoding, as shown in Fig. 1c. Moreover, the higher modulation efficiency Pancharatnam–Berry phase plate structure is processed using this approach, and a demonstration of polarization-related 3D large area information encryption is also conducted. Dc-PDLW strategy demonstrates strong potential for large-scale 3D high-duty-cycle optical phase encoding, with promising applications in diffractive optical elements, integrated photonic devices, and information encryption.
paper_content.results:
The principle of the de-coherent parallel direct laser writing process

In conventional serial laser processing, the employment of the FLDW method may be affected by the temporal sequence interference effect, resulting in the redistribution of the light field. As shown in Fig. 1d1, d2, the latter incident beam is markedly influenced by the original structure (located to the right of the latter incident beam), resulting in a shift of its peak energy and a distortion of the Gaussian distribution (Fig. 1d2), which in turn leads to a deviation from the ideal distribution of the structure produced by the latter pulse (see Supplementary Text S1 for more details).

In contrast, parallel laser processing employing holographic beam shaping generates multiple focal spots simultaneously, effectively avoiding cumulative field perturbations and material-induced non-uniformity inherent to serial exposure43,44. Particularly under tightly focused conditions (i.e., high-numerical-aperture systems), non-iterative optical phase holograms produce a uniquely determined phase distribution, ensuring uniform and stable multifocal generation without parasitic diffraction artifacts45,46. A direct comparison of the focal field distributions (under the Debye approximation, Fig. 1e) and corresponding processed structures (Fig. 1f1, f2) confirms that the iterative method induces energy redistribution and additional diffraction orders near the focus, leading to structural distortions and evident side flaps (Fig. 1f1).

Given the aforementioned considerations, we suggest a non-iterative SSP-BM algorithm, which applies stripe segmentation and binary masking to the phase hologram. The corresponding optical path is illustrated in Fig. 1e. The non-iterative phase hologram formulae for an arbitrary spatial position distribution based on the Debye diffractive electric field distribution formulae are as follows47–49 (see Supplementary Text S2 for a detailed derivation):

φM(x0, y0) = 2/λ * π * (R * NA * (Δx + Δy)) (1)

where φM is the phase loaded into SLM. Δx and Δy are the displacements of the center of focus. R is the radius of the phase plane. NA is the numerical aperture of the objective lens. nt is the material refractive index.

To achieve a high-duty-cycle, the concept of hologram partitioning is introduced. Among its forms, strip partitioning enables parallel processing of multiple focal spots while maintaining high uniformity45,50,51. Furthermore, in order to achieve a further minimization of proximity crosstalk, it is necessary to consider the effect of the phase term. A common method of reducing the effect of phase term interference is the adjustment of the polarization state36,52–59. In actual processing, the binary phase hologram is a widely utilized method for the control of polarization states at varying positions across multiple focal spots46,60. In accordance with this, we propose the combination of a binary mask with a strip segmentation phase hologram as a means of ensuring the elimination of the crosstalk generated by spatial coherence and temporal sequence interference effects (Detailed derivations are provided in the Supplementary Text S3-S4). This approach can effectively reduce the intensity fluctuations and crosstalk between spots at the nanoscale, thereby breaking the diffraction limit.

Theoretical analysis has thus far validated that SSP-BM can eliminate the effect of crosstalk, thus enabling a high-duty-cycle nanostructure via the Dc-PDLW approach incorporated with the threshold effect of multiphoton absorption, which are intuitively displayed in Fig. 1f3. A comprehensive overview is provided in Fig. 1f4, which presents the central light intensity profile. It can be observed that the GSW algorithm yields a structure with an evident side flap. In contrast, the non-iterative algorithm, although it resolves the side flap issue due to the wavefront disorder, still exhibits a similar pronounced crosstalk as the GSW algorithm. This has been effectively addressed in the SSP-BM algorithm, as evidenced by the absence of interference between the adjacent focal spots (see Supplementary Text S5 for a comparison between the non-iterative ORA algorithm and the SSP-BM algorithm).

To demonstrate the superiority of the SSP-BM algorithm, a customised structure fabricated with SSP-BM overserved by SEM images is shown in Fig. 1g. The flowchart of the hologram generation is illustrated in Fig. 1h (M denotes the number of focal spots; N denotes the number of partitions):

Step 1: Define the custom multi-focus array to be loaded, and determine M according to the number of focal spots. Then, according to the required positions, attach the corresponding XY coordinates to the focal spots in M different positions, and calculate the non-iterative phase hologram.

Step 2: Determine N partitions based on actual processing needs. Subsequently, the entire phase hologram (Main area) is divided into N partitions (Subarea). Then, the M focal spots generated in the first step are filled into the subarea.

Step 3: Generate a binary phase mask, and superpose the phase overlapped by partitions with the binary phase mask to obtain the final machining phase hologram.

Uniform parallel processing achieved via de-coherent parallel direct laser writing technology, enabling fabrication of high-duty-cycle nanopore structures

Although the feasibility of the SSP-BM algorithm has been demonstrated through theoretical calculation and simulation, the complex light-matter interactions involved in Dc-PDLW make the process considerably more challenging. The effectiveness and efficiency of the method are further evaluated in the fabrication of nanophotonic structures under various parameters. In our experiment, M=2 was chosen as the standard experimental configuration (see Supplementary Text S6-S7 for 3D demonstrations with large M).

Herein, N is a core parameter determining the fabrication performance. Figure 2a illustrates the influence of N on the uniformity of bifocal spots denoted as Q, which quantitatively describes the intensity consistency between the two beams of a dual-focus beam. Q is defined as Q = 1 - (Imax - Imin)/(Imax + Imin), where I represents the light intensity. It can be seen that the uniformity of bifocal spots exhibits an increase with N. Upon reaching N=95, the uniformity tends to reach a saturation, resulting in a uniformity value of 99.4%. (Quantitative Comparison of Bifocal Uniformity Generated by the SSP-BM Algorithm and Other Algorithms in Supplementary Table S1).

The distance between adjacent pores in the structure is a significant indicator of the efficacy of the methods employed to achieve a high-duty-cycle. The definition of spacing is given in Fig. 2b. The algorithm preset spacing and location required during processing are achieved by changing the X and Y parameters in the non-iterative phase hologram, as outlined in Eq. (1).

The deposition of laser energy into the interior of the material may result in the formation of micro-cracks, micro/nanovoids, and localised amorphisation, contingent upon the processing conditions employed. It is also essential to consider space co-operation effects in order to prevent the formation of heat-affected zones, cracks, voids, or residual stress61. Therefore, the setting of the laser parameters is particularly important in actual processing. When discussing the influence of laser energy on dual-pore spacing in actual processing, we set the algorithm preset spacing to a relatively large value to ensure a large energy interval. As the laser energy increases, the laser-induced modification region becomes larger (Fig. 2c). When the pulse energy is 550 nJ, the gap width is 879 nm, with a total width of 1412 nm. With an increase in laser energy to 850 nJ, the gap width decreases, reaching a minimum of 551 nm and a total width of 1727 nm. Accompanied by the increasing laser energy, nanopores are created at the centre of the light intensity, and a ring-shaped amorphous region is created around it due to the effect of the shock wave, which leads to an increase in the size of the nanopore structure62,63. Concurrently, the diameter of the individual nanopores within the bi-focus nanostructure increases, while the nanopore gap width is diminished as a consequence of internal squeezing. In order to achieve processing with a high-duty-cycle, it is of great interest to ascertain the minimum dual-pore spacing that a given algorithm can actually achieve during Dc-PDLW (see Supplementary Text S8 for the nanopore structure under the condition of large dual-pore spacing conditions). As the algorithm’s preset spacing decreases, we compared the processing results of the SSP-BM and the GSW algorithm. At 300 nm preset spacing, the bifocal nanopore structure processed by SSP-BM was just distinguishable (Fig. 2d1), whereas the nanopore by the GSW was not (Fig. 2d2). The slight ellipticity of the nanopore in Fig. 2d1 mainly stemmed from the vector polarization effect of linearly polarized light in a tightly focused optical system64. When the preset spacing was reduced to 200 nm—approaching the diameter of a single nanopore—both algorithms failed to resolve the two nanopores (Fig. 2d3, d4). Notably, at a further reduced preset spacing of 100 nm, the structure processed by SSP-BM remained elliptical, in contrast to the circular single nanopores obtained via the GSW (Fig. 2d5, d6).

To demonstrate the processing superiority of the SSP-BM algorithm, we performed several experiments and compared the dual-pore spacing, which appears to be distinguishable with the iterative algorithm and the unit-by-unit serial writing method under identical laser parameters (224 fs, 450 nJ). As shown in Fig. 2e, the bi-focus nanopore structure exhibits substantial concordance with the prediction of the SSP-BM algorithm, with an average value of 321 nm and a minimum observation pitch of 292 nm. In contrast, the iterative algorithm exhibits an average dual-pore spacing of 545 nm due to the disorder of the wavefront and the inability to effectively address multi-beam crosstalk, as previously discussed. The deviated effect of light field redistribution is pronounced when linearly polarized light is employed for unit-by-unit conventional serial laser processing, resulting in a larger average dual-pore spacing of 601 nm. The results illustrate the superiority of the Dc-PDLW method for realizing high-duty-cycle processing.

Meanwhile, the samples were subjected to EDS (Energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) analysis, as illustrated in Fig. 2f. This reveals that during the processing of the bifocal structure, the formation of nanostructures resulted in the original structure being compressed inwards, causing the main constituent elements Al and O in sapphire to be compressed from the outside to the center near the midpoint of the connection. Consequently, the element distribution exhibits a distinct peak at the center of the connection (superior to the outermost unmodified zone), whereas the distribution of pore elements following laser-induced modification corrosion manifests as a valley. Furthermore, the compression zone correlates with the defined gap zone65,66.

To further demonstrate the processing flexibility and superiority of Dc-PDLW, we processed dual-pore structures (Fig. 3a1–a3) and circular dual-pore arrays (Fig. 3c1, c2) based on different spacing settings (Fig. 3b). This was done to verify its efficiency in manipulating optical phase and birefringence. Additionally, it aimed to confirm that the component can serve as a unit of a birefringent device, similar to a nanofin unit. The refractive index variation of nanostructures with different dual-pore spacing was obtained by quadriwave lateral shearing interferometry67 using a wavefront phase sensor (as shown in Fig. 3a2). The results show that the maximum refractive index change of the structure after laser irradiation reached -0.25 × 10-3 (Fig. 3a3). As illustrated in Fig. 3b, the red profile line denotes the refractive index change of the large-spacing bifocal structure, and it can be observed that the refractive index curve contains a distinct double peak. As the dual-pore spacing decreases, the refractive index change becomes co-influenced by the bifocal nanostructures, as illustrated by the blue profile line, appearing as a superposition of bimodal phase delays that manifests in the form of a single peak. Fig. 3c1-c2 illustrates a circular dual-pore array structure that demonstrates the large-scale, 3D phase and birefringence encoding capabilities of the Dc-PDLW method. Therefore, decreasing dual-pore spacing enhances the duty cycle and refractive index modulation, establishing a basis for birefringent structure fabrication. The compact system architecture of Dc-PDLW benefits from the employment of SLM, making it fully scalable in mass production. During the large-scale processing of a micro-nano birefringent device, it takes less than 3 min to achieve a complete phase encoding process (2x2 mm). The high processing rate of micro- and nano-optical products demonstrates the great potential and full feasibility of Dc-PDLW technology in practical applications.

Applications of de-coherent parallel direct laser writing technology

From an application perspective, the proposed Dc-PDLW approach introduces a fundamentally new class of anisotropic dual-pore nanostructures that are significantly different from existing laser-induced anisotropic structures, such as self-assembled nanogratings68,69, type-X birefringent structures70, and isotropic nanovoids71. Unlike these prior methods, which rely on multi-pulse accumulation or near-field enhancement and consequently suffer from limited controllability and scalability, our SSP-BM-based strategy achieves subwavelength features with a single pulse, enabling predictable birefringence tuning, high uniformity, and precise polarisation encoding. Beyond its technical innovation, this method provides complete freedom in polarization optics design, allowing simultaneous control over both birefringence magnitude (Fig. 1c) and optical-axis orientation (Fig. 4b), and underscoring the strong potential of this approach for high-density, polarization-resolved optical storage and advanced photonic device fabrication.

The Dc-PDLW method can be efficiently extended from a point into line-like structures, enabling the inscription of 3D photonic devices. At the same time, this technology is employed to generate dense, highly integrated diffraction gratings (Fig. 4a), where hologram control allows precise regulation of the grating period (d). A decrease in the grating period leads to an increase in the diffraction angle. For periods of d=1 μm and d=2.5 μm, the diffraction angles are measured to be 0.14 and 0.05, respectively. The resulting curve agrees well with the grating diffraction formula. Further results on the influence of laser energy on gratings can be found in Supplementary Text S9.

Another important application lies in geometric phase and polarization encoding, which can be achieved through space-variant retardance engineered in Dc-PDLW–inscribed anisotropic nanostructures (see Supplementary Text S10 for more details). Benefiting from the de-coherent parallel processing nature of Dc-PDLW, the inter-feature spacing can be significantly reduced, enabling stronger and more precise refractive-index modulation for accurate phase and polarization control. Here, by employing the Dc-PLDW method to modulate the dual-pore spacing and relative orientation of the bifocal nanostructure, equivalent to the engineering of birefringence and the rotation of the optical axis, a polarization-selective grating (Pancharatnam–Berry phase plate structure) is processed70,72,73. Figure 4b shows structures fabricated with a sub-diffraction spacing using the SSP-BM algorithm (~500 nm, the right inset of Fig. 4b), thereby demonstrating that our Dc-PDLW method can reliably achieve super-resolution machining of large-area 3D diffractive optical elements. Bifocal nanostructures tilted at different azimuthal angles at different locations were sequentially written until a 180-degree cycle is completed, as illustrated in the upper left inset of Fig. 4c. Besides, it can be observed that under orthogonal linearly polarized light, different parts of the PB phase plate structure exhibit different brightness. Modifying the angle of the orthogonally polarized light results in a change in the intensity of the light-dark cycle of the structure due to polarization sensitivity, as shown in the right inset of Fig. 4c.

Given that the different spacing and relative orientation of bifocal nanostructures present varying degrees of light intensity under polarized light illumination, this property can be exploited for the encryption of polarization-related information74–76. As shown in Fig. 4d, two messages that include a QR code and an image of a qiushie eagle are inscribed overlapped but with different azimuthal angles. It is evident that when observed through natural light illumination, the QR code information is partially obscured by the eagle pattern, rendering it unreadable. Under a correct observation condition with orthogonal polarized light at 45° and 135°, the encrypted information can be displayed clearly. Figure 4e provides another example of the encryption of messages within a QR code, whereby only the requisite azimuth angle is inscribed within the designated square area. The remaining portion of the square is fixed with dual-pore structures, oriented at an angle that is orthogonal to the inscribed angle. As can be observed, when the image is viewed under natural light, the entire pattern appears completely unreadable. In contrast, when the image is viewed under orthogonally polarized light at 45° and 135°, the QR code information appears readable. The results demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing the Dc-PDLW method for the encryption of polarization-related information (see more demonstrations in Supplementary Text S11–S13).

In conclusion, we have proposed a de-coherent parallel direct laser writing (Dc-PDLW) strategy for the inscription of a nanopore array with an ultra-dense distribution, which is achieved by superimposing a non-iterative strip segmentation phase hologram combined with a binary phase mask, in conjunction with wet etching, to create a nanopore structure with a high-duty processing cycle. The principle of achieving super-resolution and crosstalk cancellation using this method has been elucidated and investigated. The non-iterative process eliminates the wavefront disorder of the iterative algorithm, and partitions combined with a binary phase mask eliminate crosstalk generated by spatial coherence and temporal sequence interference effects, thereby ensuring that the feature size of the spacing is in the subwavelength region. The efficiency of the Dc-PDLW is demonstrated by the production of a 3D large-area PB phase plate structure, which exhibits excellent diffraction efficiency and polarization sensitivity. Dc-PDLW exhibits remarkable 3D large-area optical phase encoding capabilities, which portend significant potential for applications in the domain of information encryption. It is particularly well-suited for inscribing meticulously designed phase encodings with nanoscale feature sizes and high efficiencies in a diverse array of materials. Concurrently, the minimum dual-pore spacing is anticipated to be diminished further, potentially through the deployment of larger NA objectives or the utilization of shorter processing wavelengths. The proposed method will facilitate further development of encrypted messages, computational holography, optical storage, and integrated photonics.
paper_content.methods:
Sample preparation

In our experiments, commercially available Z-cut bulk sapphire wafers with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 0.2 mm (thickness) and full-side polishing were employed. For the fabrication of dual-pore structures, the laser energy was adjusted to a level slightly above the modification energy threshold of sapphire, inducing modification at a depth of 50 μm beneath the sapphire surface. Subsequent to modification, the upper surface of the sapphire was polished until the modified structure was completely exposed.

Ultrafast Laser Processing System

The experimental setup of the femtosecond laser processing system is illustrated in Figure S1. A femtosecond laser system (Pharos, Light Conversion Ltd.) with a pulse duration of 224 fs, a repetition rate of 10 kHz, and a central wavelength of 1030 nm was employed. The polarization of the laser beam was controlled by rotating a half-wave plate (HWP1). Subsequently, the phase hologram was loaded into the liquid crystal SLM (spatial light modulator, Hamamatsu LCOS X13138 series, reflection-type) in order to generate multiple focal spots with a nano-scale distance. A 4f system was constructed by employing two lenses with focal lengths of 400 mm (L1) and 600 mm (L2), respectively. HWP2 coordinates the binary phase mask to achieve an orthogonal polarization state. Subsequently, the beam is focused 50 µm below the sapphire sample surface using an oil immersion objective with a numerical aperture (NA) of 1.25. A CCD camera was employed to assess the uniformity of the multifocal light spot. The sapphire samples were mounted on a 3D translation stage (SmarAct), which provides a positioning resolution of 1 nm.

Structural Characterization

After fabrication, the sapphire samples were preliminarily examined under an optical microscope (Olympus BX53M). The fine structures were further characterized through a SEM (scanning electron microscope, Zeiss), after polishing and etching (40% HF, 80°C, 60 min). Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis was performed simultaneously with the SEM measurements on the same region of the sample, enabling in-situ elemental composition characterization while acquiring structural information. The optical phase difference of dual-pore arrays were mearsured by quadriwave lateral shearing interferometry using a wavefront phase sensor (Phasics Sid4).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper proposed a new method that enabled multi-beam parallel processing with a spacing between adjacent two beams (point spacing) of less than 1/3 of the laser wavelength. The authors presented both theoretical and experimental approaches to validate the capabilities of the proposed method with demonstrations of several related applications. The technique is useful for fabricating 3D photonic devices with high throughput through parallel processing. Therefore, the reviewer considers that this manuscript can be accepted for publication in Nature Communications, but some major revisions based on the following comments are required before being accepted.
Major Comments:
Paper title:
The title of the paper sounds like it does not do justice to the content of this paper. The reviewer feels that “multi-beam parallel processing” is much more important than “single-pulse laser pattering”.
Line 119:
What does “the latter incident beam” mean? Are two beams incident with some delay time? If yes, how long is the delay time? In this process, two beams must be simultaneously incident.
Fig. 2 d1:
Both nanopores appear to be transversely elongated elliptical in shape. Why not circle?
Fig. 2 f (lower):
EDS measurement must have been done after the chemical etching. If so, the low-density regions should be removed by the etching (in fact, nanopores are created in the SEM image). Why is the relative content at the nanopores still lower than that at the surrounding areas (< 100 nm and > 1200 nm)?
Lines 273 – 276
In my understanding, the unit-by-unit writing means the single beam processing, right? If so, why is the deviation effect of the redistribution of the optical field caused by spatial coherence more pronounced in the single-beam processing?
Applications
The authors demonstrated thee applications of diffraction gratings, a polarization-selective grating (Pancharatnam–Berry phase plate structure), and encrypted QR Codes. However, all elements look like being fabricated with pointing spacings much larger than 1/3 of the laser wavelength. To show the superiority of this technique over the other techniques, all elements should be fabricated with a pointing spacing smaller than 1/3 of the laser wavelength.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This study presents a novel approach to overcoming the diffraction limit in parallel laser processing using femtosecond laser pulses. This research introduces the de-coherent parallel direct laser writing (Dc-PDLW) strategy, which utilizes a combination of a patterned single pulse and a de-coherent holographic algorithm to surpass the traditional diffraction limit in multi-beam laser processing. By effectively managing spatial coherence and temporal sequence interference, the study achieves a resolution of 300 nm (~λ/4), setting a record for parallel laser processing.
There has been a recent push in the field to explore the limits of laser processing using this general approach, but I have not seen this specific methodology i.e.non-iterative strip segmentation phase holograms which avoid uneven energy distribution, and binary masks to customize polarization states and eliminate coherence between focal points. The work is potentially a breakthrough contribution from the authors. The significance of this work is underlined by its application to produce large area three-dimensional structures such as Pancharatnam–Berry phase plates and voluminous cipher sequences, demonstrating advanced high-density phase and polarization coding capabilities in 3D.
I believe this is a significant breakthrough expands the potential of femtosecond laser processing for complex, high-resolution micro- and nano-fabrication tasks.
It is excellent work and worthy of rapid publication. However, I may suggest (optionally) that the authors consider including comments on the implementation of the Dc-PDLW approach. This clearly involves a sophisticated and precise setup, requiring advanced optical components and meticulous alignment. Whilst this may be possible with unlimited research time, does this limit the approach's potential application and scalability? Is it indeed possible to scale the technique for large-scale production. A few comments (in the conclusions perhaps) would be useful here.
The work is very well written, nicely presented and extensively referenced. There a just a few grammatical and typo errors which need addressing.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Reviewer Comments – Recommendation: Reject
The submitted manuscript presents a study on the fabrication of ultradense nanopore arrays using a de-coherent parallel direct laser writing (Dc-PDLW) strategy based on a non-iterative strip segmentation phase hologram combined with a binary phase mask (SSP-BM). The authors claim that this method improves uniformity and reduces crosstalk in multi-focus femtosecond laser processing, enabling high-resolution structures and polarization-sensitive encoding.
The manuscript demonstrates certain technical merit, such as the integration of polarization control and holographic beam shaping. Therefore, the paper has some scientific value as it experimentally confirms that the SSP-BM approach can fabricate subwavelength structures with a specific polarization control strategy.
However, I must conclude that the novelty and significance of the work are insufficient for publication in Nature Communications, due to the following critical concerns:
1. Lack of originality in concept:
The proposed method is conceptually similar to previous works [1,2], which have already demonstrated polarization control in parallel femtosecond laser processing using spatial light modulators. The approach adopted in this manuscript does not significantly depart from those existing methods, and the incremental improvement offered is relatively modest.
2. Overstated limitations of iterative algorithms:
The authors criticize iterative hologram design methods, such as the Gerchberg–Saxton (GS) algorithm, for introducing wavefront disorder. However, they overlook important developments in improved iterative methods, such as the Weighted GS (WGS) algorithm, which effectively suppresses multi-beam inhomogeneity. These improved techniques can generate high-uniformity multifocal arrays and should not be dismissed without quantitative comparison.
3. Low diffraction efficiency likely due to polarization geometry:
The proposed system uses a 45° linearly polarized beam incident on a liquid crystal on silicon (LCOS) SLM with a binary phase mask. Given this optical configuration, the diffraction efficiency is likely very low. In practical laser processing applications, especially those requiring high throughput and energy efficiency, low-efficiency holograms are generally unacceptable.
4. Resolution claims are not surprising given known nonlinear effects:
The reported spatial resolution of 300 nm (approximately λ/4) is attributed to the suppression of crosstalk via polarization control. However, such resolution is not unprecedented in femtosecond laser processing due to nonlinear absorption and threshold effects. Therefore, the result is not as remarkable as the authors suggest.
In conclusion, although the authors have provided some experimental validation of the SSP-BM method, the conceptual novelty, technical innovation, and impact are insufficient to meet the high standard of Nature Communications. The paper would be more appropriate for a specialized journal focused on laser fabrication or applied optics.
References:
[1] S. Hasegawa and Y. Hayasaki, "Polarization distribution control of parallel femtosecond pulses with spatial light modulators," Opt. Express 21, 12987–12995 (2013).
[2] S. Hasegawa and Y. Hayasaki, "Holographic Vector Wave Femtosecond Laser Processing," Int. J. Optomechatronics 8, 73–88 (2014).

Question 2: Fig. 2 d1:
Both nanopores appear to be transversely elongated elliptical in shape. Why not circle?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question. The slight
ellipticity observed in Fig. 2d1 arises from a combination of optical and spatial interference
effects inherent to multi-beam parallel femtosecond laser processing. Specifically:
1. Crosstalk effects in linearly arranged multi-focus arrays:
The elongation arises primarily from the coherent crosstalk between neighboring foci
generated by the spatial light modulator (SLM). When the focal points are arranged along a straight
line, the corresponding phase hologram exhibits periodicity analogous to a circular moiré pattern
due to the regular grid alignment. After Fourier transformation by the objective lens, this periodic
structure leads to localized energy convergence along the connecting line between adjacent foci,
producing elliptical rather than circular energy distributions at the focus [Opto-Electronic Advances
7, 240082 (2024); Optics Letters 30,2086-2088 (2005).]. This effect becomes more pronounced as
the inter-spot spacing decreases or the number of foci increases.
2. Distribution geometry effects:
We have verified that when using a non-collinear (e.g., triangular, Fig. R1(a1-a2, b1-b2))
spatial distribution of foci, this crosstalk effect is effectively suppressed, resulting in nearly circular
nanopores. This phenomenon can be attributed to the fact that the aggregated crosstalk of the three
points is partially canceled out due to the triangular distribution. This observation is consistent with
our supplementary data (Fig. S12c3), where nonuniform and triangular distributions yield improved
roundness and uniformity.
Figure R1. (a1-a2) Optical micrographs of close-up 3-pore structures with (b1-b2) corresponding
SEMs. Scale bars: 500 nm. Both optical and electron microscopy confirm that the fabricated
nanopores exhibit excellent circular symmetry. (c–d) Comparison between simulated and
experimentally observed focal spot profiles at different numerical apertures (NA). It is revealed that
under high-NA focusing conditions (NA > 0.8), a slight asymmetry (maximum ellipticity ≈ 1.12) may
occur due to the vectorial nature of tightly focused linearly polarized light.
3.Effect of Debye diffraction：
The generation of SSP-BM holograms is based on Debye diffraction theory, which inherently
accounts for high-NA focusing conditions and partially corrects the associated aberrations.
Nevertheless, due to the substantial numerical aperture (NA) of the processing objective, a minor
residual asymmetry in the focal field distribution can persist. As a result, slight ellipsoidal features
(with a maximum ellipticity of approximately 1.12) are occasionally observed when linearly
polarized light is employed [Acta Physica Sinica 61, 234202-234202 (2012)].
Importantly, this weak ellipticity does not negatively impact the birefringence magnitude
or polarization sensitivity of the fabricated structures. The birefringence strength in our
approach is primarily governed by the focal spacing and processing period, rather than by the
minor asymmetry of individual focal spots. As experimentally confirmed in Fig. 4, the overall
polarization-resolved response of the fabricated birefringent devices remains highly stable and
uniform, demonstrating that the observed ellipticity is negligible for both structural
functionality and optical performance.
Question 3: Fig. 2 f (lower):
EDS measurement must have been done after the chemical etching. If so, the low-density

Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. Indeed, the EDS analysis
was performed after chemical etching. The observed difference in elemental distribution arises
from two combined effects: structural extrusion at the pore boundaries and signal attenuation
caused by the nanopore cavity, as explained below.
1. Structural extrusion in the edge region (< 100 nm and > 1200 nm).
During nanopore formation, the femtosecond-laser-induced shock wave expands radially
outward from the focal center, leading to local structural extrusion in the surrounding material
[Physical Review Letters 96, 166101 (2006)]. The central region experiences the strongest
compression and material transformation, while the adjacent regions are partially squeezed outward
by the shock wave [Advanced Materials 18, 1361-1364 (2006).]. After wet etching, the highly
modified amorphous region at the center is selectively removed to form the nanopore cavity. The
edge regions, however, undergo densification or even transient high-pressure phase formation
during the shock-induced extrusion process, making them more resistant to etching. As a result,
these edge regions exhibit relatively higher elemental signal intensity in the post-etching EDS maps,
consistent with our measurements. The schematic diagram of shock wave diffusion during
processing is shown in Fig. R2.
Figure R2. Schematic diagram of the direction of shock wave diffusion and compression during
formation of the nanopore. The yellow arrow indicates the direction of shock wave propagation.
2. EDS signal attenuation caused by the nanopore cavity.
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) detects element-specific X-rays generated by
high-energy electron excitation. However, nanoscale cavity structures can obstruct or scatter the
emitted X-rays, thereby weakening the detected signal from the nanopore region. This geometric
attenuation effect causes the apparent elemental content at the nanopore center to appear lower than
that of the surrounding dense material, even though the actual composition difference may be
negligible.
Question 4: Lines 273 – 276
In my understanding, the unit-by-unit writing means the single beam processing, right? If so, why

Response: Thank you for these insightful questions. Yes, the unit-by-unit writing means the
single-beam processing or serial laser processing method.
The spatial-coherence–induced deviation arises from the interference between the incident
laser field and the field scattered by pre-existing nanopores. Specifically, the first laser pulse forms
a nanopore within the material. After a delay longer than the cavity-formation time (>1 ms, allowing
full cooling and solidification), a subsequent pulse is delivered nearby, with a center-to-center
spacing of <0.61 λ/NA. This second pulse encounters the scattering field from the existing nanopore,
and the interference between the two fields redistributes the local optical intensity, shifting the
location of the peak intensity (Fig. 1 d1-d2). Numerical simulations confirm that this effect becomes
stronger and the positional deviation more pronounced as the inter-pore spacing decreases or the
nanopore diameter increases (also see in [Advanced Functional Materials 34, 11 (2024) 2306870.]).
In single-beam serial processing, each pulse arrives sequentially and is therefore inevitably
affected by the residual structural modifications produced by the preceding pulse (Fig. S2).
Consequently, the spatial-coherence-induced optical-field redistribution and associated positional
deviation are more pronounced in serial (unit-by-unit) processing [Light: Science & Applications 9,
41 (2020)].
In contrast, the parallel laser processing method involves the simultaneous incidence of multiple
beams, rather than sequential delivery. At this timescale, the formation of a strongly scattering
nanopore has not yet occurred (the structural formation happens on microsecond–millisecond
timescales). The transient plasma generated during the femtosecond exposure induces only a weak,
symmetric refractive index modulation (Δn < 0.03) [Nat Photonics 18, 799-808 (2024)], far smaller
than the Δn ≈ 0.76 contrast of a nanopore, and thus does not introduce inter-beam field redistribution.
Therefore, the deviation caused by field redistribution is negligible in parallel processing.

nonlinear threshold effect of femtosecond pulses, which enables the fabrication of nanostructures with
sub-100-nanometer features [37-41].”
Figure R2. (a1-a2) Optical micrographs of close-up 3-pore structures with (b1-b2)
corresponding SEMs. Scale bars: 500 nm.
c) Broader application perspective:
In previous studies (including [1,2]), laser-induced polarization-dependent structures (such
as nanogratings) have been primarily utilized for fabricating diffractive optical elements and
optical data storage, where multi-beam parallel processing was introduced mainly to enhance
processing or read/write efficiency. Such approaches have been extensively reported across
various material systems [Laser Photonics Rev 2024, 18, 2300891.
https://doi.org/10.1002/lpor.202300891]. Here, we would like to clarify the key distinctions
between these previous works and the present study, by emphasizing the application-driven
novelty of our work:
(1) Advantages for encrypted optical storage:
Compared with existing anisotropic nanostructures, such as laser-induced self-assembled
nanogratings, type-X birefringent structures, and burst-mode few-pulse isotropic nanovoids—
our dual-pore approach offers substantial improvements in fabrication efficiency, polarization
control precision, and reproducibility:
 Self-assembled nanogratings require multiple pulses, produce feature sizes of several
microns, and exhibit lower duty cycles. Their formation relies on near-field
enhancement and multiphysics coupling, which are often material-dependent and
unpredictable, whereas our approach uses a single pulse to achieve subwavelength (<1
μm) features with linear, predictable birefringence tuning.
 Type-X birefringent structures also require multiple pulses and typically yield feature
sizes from several to tens of microns, far larger than the dense nanopores achieved
here.
 Burst-mode isotropic nanovoids depend on complex intracavity or extracavity pulse
shaping and still rely on near-field effects, limiting their controllability and scalability.
In contrast, our SSP-BM strategy circumvents near-field instabilities, ensuring both
uniform modifications and accurate polarization encoding.
(2) Advantages for non-encrypted storage and beyond:
In applications such as Braille-like records (Supplementary Fig. S12), our approach
demonstrates further advantages:
 The overall pattern size can be significantly reduced.
 The uniformity of each nanopore ensures a very low error rate in information retrieval,
highlighting the reliability of our encoding strategy.
Together, these aspects underline that our contribution is not simply an incremental
technical refinement. Instead, it opens a new pathway for scalable, high-density, polarization-
resolved optical storage and phase encoding, with strong implications for both practical
devices and fundamental photonics research.
(3) Full freedom in polarization optics design:
By introducing dual-pore anisotropic nanostructures as the elementary units, our method
allows simultaneous and precise control over both birefringence magnitude and optical-axis
orientation. This capability provides the complete set of degrees of freedom required for the
design and fabrication of polarization diffraction optical elements, which has not been
achievable with previous laser-written structures.
(Lines 306-317) “From an application perspective, the proposed Dc-PDLW approach
introduces a fundamentally new class of anisotropic dual-pore nanostructures that are significantly
different from existing laser-induced anisotropic structures, such as self-assembled nanogratings68,
69, type-X birefringent structures70, and isotropic nanovoids71. Unlike these prior methods, which
rely on multi-pulse accumulation or near-field enhancement and consequently suffer from limited
controllability and scalability, our SSP-BM-based strategy achieves subwavelength features with a
single pulse, enabling predictable birefringence tuning, high uniformity, and precise polarization
encoding. Beyond its technical innovation, this method provides complete freedom in polarization

density, polarization-resolved optical storage and advanced photonic device fabrication.”
In summary, while our work builds upon the foundational principle of SLM-based
polarization control, it advances the field substantially by (i) identifying and overcoming the
fundamental spacing limitation in parallel laser writing, (ii) introducing a decoherence-based
holographic strategy with high energy efficiency and flexibility, and (iii) demonstrating new
classes of ultradense, functionally encoded 3D nanostructures.
Reviewer Comment 2 / 4
Concern 2: Overstated limitations of iterative algorithms:
The authors criticize iterative hologram design methods, such as the Gerchberg–Saxton (GS)
algorithm, for introducing wavefront disorder. However, they overlook important
developments in improved iterative methods, such as the Weighted GS (WGS) algorithm, which
effectively suppresses multi-beam inhomogeneity. These improved techniques can generate
high-uniformity multifocal arrays and should not be dismissed without quantitative comparison.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully agree
that iterative hologram design methods such as the Gerchberg–Saxton (GS) and Weighted GS
(WGS) algorithms have made important contributions to achieving high-uniformity multifocal
arrays. The WGS algorithm, in particular, effectively suppresses beam inhomogeneity and has
been successfully applied in various holographic beam-shaping scenarios.
However, it is important to note that the GS/WGS algorithms are primarily designed for phase
shaping, and cannot independently control the polarization states of individual foci. Therefore, they
are unsuitable for investigating the core scientific problem addressed in our study: the fundamental
limit of spacing between adjacent foci in parallel laser processing and its determining factors. As
emphasized in our response to Comment 1, the present work goes far beyond a mere algorithmic
improvement. It addresses a conceptual problem that has not been previously explored. Hence,
while we have retained the necessary comparisons to highlight methodological distinctions, we have
deliberately streamlined discussions of algorithmic performance to maintain the manuscript’s focus
on the fundamental physical and processing insights. In the revised manuscript, we have
intentionally avoided excessive discussion on the relative merits of different algorithms, as such
debate deviates from the central focus of our study. Instead, we have streamlined and downplayed
this part, while adding Table S1 to provide a clear quantitative comparison.
(Lines 65-82) “Among these methods, the WGS/GSW iterative algorithm has great flexibility and
the best parallel beam uniformity, making it a widely-used method for generating complex multi-beams
patterns. However, it is important to note that GSW algorithms do not uniquely determine the phase
during the iteration process, which can lead to wavefront disorder that may degrade processing
performance[30-34], especially under high numerical aperture (NA) focusing conditions. In particular,
in the context of this study, where adjacent focal spots are brought into extremely close proximity and
their optical fields begin to overlap, this wavefront disorder can induce complex spatial coherence effects,
making it difficult to surpass the coherent diffraction limit that constrains the minimum achievable
spacing between adjacent spots (≈1.47λ/NA) [35]. Furthermore, by controlling the polarization
orthogonality between adjacent beams, the spatial coherence effects of the optical fields can be
effectively eliminated, thereby reducing the minimum achievable spacing between adjacent focal spots
by half (≈0.73λ/NA) [36], approaching the coherent diffraction limit. However, in multi-focus parallel
femtosecond laser processing, the spacing between adjacent focal points has consistently been
constrained by the coherent diffraction limit. In contrast, single-focus femtosecond laser processing can
readily surpass this limitation owing to the strong nonlinear threshold effect of femtosecond pulses, which
enables the fabrication of nanostructures with sub-100-nanometer features [37-41].”
Furthermore, in order to clarify the motivation of this research, Fig. R1 presents a
fabricated “Siemens Test Star” consisting of periodic dual-pore arrays with gradually
decreasing spacing from the outer to the inner regions, produced using double beams with
identical polarization (generated by GSW algorithm) and orthogonal polarization (generated by
SSP-BM algorithm) states. This figure provides a direct visual comparison of the processing
resolution achievable with and without polarization control in dual-beam parallel fabrication.
The results reveal the intrinsic limitation of coherent multi-beam irradiation imposed by the
coherent diffraction limit: in the coherent FLDW case, the central region (indicated by a red
circle in Fig. R1(a)) exhibits complex, high-frequency interference-like patterns, with the
maximum resolvable spatial frequency reaching v₀; in contrast, the non-coherent FLDW
configuration yields a much clearer central region (marked by a red circle in Fig. R1(b)), where
the maximum resolvable spatial frequency is reduced to v₀/2. These observations clearly
demonstrate how varying degrees of coherence fundamentally influence the achievable
processing resolution in parallel femtosecond laser fabrication.
Figure R1. Fabricated “Siemens Test Star” composed of periodic dual-pore arrays with gradually
decreasing dual-pore spacing from the outer to the inner regions, produced using double beams with
(a) identical polarization and (b) orthogonal polarization states.
Additionally, from the standpoint of tightly focused femtosecond laser processing, iterative
algorithms still face intrinsic limitations. As shown in Fig. S12c1-c2, even WGS-based
holograms exhibit residual speckle noise and ghost images under high-NA focusing conditions,
leading to reduced stability and reproducibility during material processing. Moreover, because
iterative algorithms cannot uniquely determine the phase during convergence, they are prone to
wavefront disorder and local-optimum trapping. These issues become particularly pronounced
when adjacent foci are closely spaced and their focal fields begin to overlap, which severely
limits the achievable density of parallel processing (Fig. R1).
Fig. S12 c1-c2. Simulation comparison of machining letters generated using the SSP-BM algorithm
and the GSW algorithm. (Note: Although the WGS method can generate high uniformity of peak
intensity through optimization, but speckle artifacts are difficult to avoid in tight focusing conditions.
In contrast, the suggested SSP-BM approach can address the problem of speckle artifacts, enabling better
fabrication quality)
In contrast, our proposed SSP-BM algorithm—based on a non-iterative design—uniquely
determines the phase distribution in a single computational step, effectively avoiding both the
speckle noise problem and the local convergence issue. Moreover, by introducing a strip-
segmentation and binary-mask strategy, SSP-BM enables localized polarization control for each
beam, a capability fundamentally beyond the reach of iterative algorithms. A quantitative discussion
comparing the algorithms has been added to the Table. S1, that SSP-BM shows its superiority in
terms of uniformity, in addition to the flexible control of multiple focuses and the efficiency of
hologram generation, offering greater advantages in actual processing.
Table. S1. Quantitative comparison between the SSP-BM algorithm and the iterative algorithm GS, as
well as the optimized iterative algorithm GSW/WGS, and the non-iterative algorithm ORA (Holograms
for comparing homogeneity for generating close point pairs).
Reviewer Comment 3 / 4
Concern 3: Low diffraction efficiency likely due to polarization geometry
The proposed system uses a 45° linearly polarized beam incident on a liquid crystal on
silicon (LCOS) SLM with a binary phase mask. Given this optical configuration, the diffraction
efficiency is likely very low. In practical laser processing applications, especially those
requiring high throughput and energy efficiency, low-efficiency holograms are generally
unacceptable.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding diffraction efficiency in the
proposed optical configuration. In our system, when a 45° linearly polarized beam is incident on the
liquid crystal on silicon (LCOS) spatial light modulator (SLM), approximately 50% of the incident
light is modulated by the SLM (as detailed in Supplementary Text S4), while the remaining 50%—
corresponding to the orthogonal polarization component—remains as the zero-order beam with a
polarization state of either 0° or 90°. When the zero-order beam is filtered out and only the
modulated portion is used for processing, the effective diffraction efficiency is 50% × 97% (the
transmittance of the SLM), resulting in an overall efficiency of approximately 48.5%. Alternatively,
when the zero-order beam is intentionally utilized as one of the processing foci, the overall
diffraction efficiency can reach 97%. Besides, the experimental measurement of the ratio of the
energy after the objective lens to the energy incident on the SLM shows that the overall efficiency
of the system is 25% and 44% respectively. Therefore, the proposed method achieves an energy
utilization efficiency no lower than 25%, which is well within the acceptable range for parallel
femtosecond laser processing systems.
Moreover, the typical pulse energy required to fabricate the dual-pore nanostructures
demonstrated in this work is on the order of hundreds of nanojoules per pulse—significantly lower
than both the peak pulse energy of commercial femtosecond laser systems (typically on the order of
hundreds of microjoules) and the damage threshold of the SLM (greater than 700 W/cm²). This
enables single-shot fabrication of many dual-pore units simultaneously (for example, a 10 × 10
array as shown in Fig. S6), resulting in a two-order-of-magnitude enhancement in processing
throughput compared with single-beam scanning approaches.
Fig. S6. (a) Phase hologram and (b) optical microscopy image of a 10×10 dense array
fabricated using Dc-PDLW.
Therefore, we believe that the polarization geometry adopted in this work does not necessarily
lead to low diffraction efficiency. Instead, the overall optical configuration achieves an optimal
balance between energy utilization, processing throughput, and system simplicity.
Reviewer Comment 4 / 4
Concern 4: Resolution claims are not surprising given known nonlinear effects
The reported spatial resolution of 300 nm (approximately λ/4) is attributed to the
suppression of crosstalk via polarization control. However, such resolution is not
unprecedented in femtosecond laser processing due to nonlinear absorption and
threshold effects. Therefore, the result is not as remarkable as the authors suggest.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comment. We fully agree that
nonlinear threshold effects are well known to enable sub-diffraction feature sizes in isolated
single-spot femtosecond laser processing. However, our work addresses a fundamentally
different limitation—namely, the minimum achievable spacing between adjacent foci in
parallel multi-beam processing. In conventional multi-focus configurations, the spacing
between adjacent spots has long been constrained by the coherent diffraction limit. In contrast,
the nonlinear threshold effect in single-focus fabrication determines the minimum feature size
of an isolated modification. These two mechanisms play complementary roles: the nonlinear
threshold effect defines how small an individual feature can be, whereas our de-coherent
parallel writing strategy determines how closely adjacent features can be positioned within a
dense array.
By introducing orthogonal polarization states and suppressing both spatial coherence and
temporal sequence interference, our SSP-BM approach effectively eliminates crosstalk
between neighboring beams, allowing the spot-to-spot spacing to shrink below the conventional
λ/2 barrier—approaching the coherence-free limit of λ/4. This capability bridges the gap
between sub-diffraction single-spot resolution and large-area, high-throughput multi-spot
fabrication. While sub-λ/4 features have been achieved in isolated single-spot configurations,
extending such resolution uniformly across parallel arrays has not been previously
demonstrated. Therefore, our work does not merely replicate nonlinear shrinkage effects, but
rather establishes a new framework that brings sub-diffraction precision into scalable, de-
coherent, large-area femtosecond laser fabrication.
Furthermore, the synergy between Dc-PDLW (de-coherent parallel direct laser writing)
and the nonlinear threshold effect enables both subwavelength feature sizes and subwavelength
inter-spot spacing (see Fig. R2 and Fig. 4b), achieving truly ultradense nanoscale structuring
that has not been realized in previous polarization-controlled studies.
(Lines 78-82) “However, in multi-focus parallel femtosecond laser processing, the spacing between
adjacent focal points has consistently been constrained by the coherent diffraction limit. In contrast,
single-focus femtosecond laser processing can readily surpass this limitation owing to the strong
nonlinear threshold effect of femtosecond pulses, which enables the fabrication of nanostructures with
sub-100-nanometer features [37-41].”
Figure R2. (a1-a2) Optical micrographs of close-up 3-pore structures with (b1-b2)
corresponding SEMs. Scale bars: 500 nm.
Therefore, the proposed Dc-PDLW strategy is compatible with and complementary to the
nonlinear threshold effect of ultrafast laser–matter interaction, rather than contradictory to it.
Reviewer Comment
In conclusion, although the authors have provided some experimental validation
of the SSP-BM method, the conceptual novelty, technical innovation, and impact are
insufficient to meet the high standard of Nature Communications. The paper would be
more appropriate for a specialized journal focused on laser fabrication or applied
optics.
Response: Thank you again for your careful review. We believe our detailed responses to all
four concerns and the accompanying revisions strengthen the manuscript’s novelty and impact. We
respectfully ask that you reconsider our submission for Nature Communications.
